changelog_1_4: [SUPERSEDED SAME DAY by 1.5 — see changelog_1_5. The C&W-hard operative benchmark described here was ratified and then RETIRED on 2026-07-14. Retained for audit trail only. DO NOT SCREEN OFF IT.] GABRIEL RATIFIED THE BASIS BENCHMARK (2026-07-14, governor-level, explicitly authorised). The basis hard floor now tests against C&W 2025 SMALL-TIER HARD COST, per metro, replacing the unsourced $140/$170/$150/$130 figures. Per-metro floors (75% of replacement): Columbus $97.88 · Cincinnati $107.36 · Kansas City $97.45 · Indianapolis $107.59 · Maryland $100.27 · Madison $97.54 · Grand Rapids $107.73 · Richmond $100.27 · Des Moines $98.59. Net effect: Maryland tightens 21%, Richmond 11%, Columbus/KC/Madison ~7%; Cincinnati/Indianapolis/Grand Rapids loosen ~2-3%; Des Moines flat. Re-screening all 28 priced candidates from the 2026-07-14 scan flipped exactly TWO — 700 Kane St and 2800 Annapolis Rd, both Baltimore, both PASS -> FAIL-BASIS. Rejected the all-in denominator: it would set the floor at ~$172/SF, which all 17 priced Midwest/MD deals clear — a floor that passes 17 of 17 is not a floor. The all-in figure ($200-240/SF true replacement) is retained as an IC-MEMO narrative point, not a gate.
changelog_1_2: Added replacement_cost_doctrine (top-level) + a per-cluster replacement_cost block to all 9 clusters. Driven by a 2026-07-14 finding that ORA's operative basis-floor benchmarks ($140 Midwest / $170 MD / $150 Richmond / $130 DSM) were NEVER SOURCED — and the basis floor is the primary acquisition gate. Sourcing pass produced defensible (DERIVED) hard-cost figures for only 3 of 9 metros; the other 6 are recorded as UNSOURCED rather than interpolated. Also added: KC flood-district DD flag, Montgomery County MD coverage downgrade (monthly), Madison thin-inventory confirmation.
changelog_1_3: GABRIEL SUPPLIED THE PRIMARY SOURCE — the Cushman & Wakefield 2025 Industrial Construction Cost Guide (46 Americas markets, March 2025 costs). Hard cost is now SOURCED for 5 of 9 ORA metros directly from its Local Market Data tables (Columbus $130.51, Cincinnati $143.15, Kansas City $129.94, Indianapolis $143.46, Baltimore $133.70); the other 4 (Madison, Grand Rapids, Richmond, Des Moines) are NOT in the guide and now carry explicit [PROXY] figures. THREE FINDINGS: (1) our $140 Midwest was a good hard-cost proxy (within ~7%); (2) our $170 MARYLAND was 27% TOO HIGH — Baltimore is a mid-priced market, and this error wrongly cleared two Baltimore deals on the 2026-07-14 scan; (3) the guide's own size curve (cost ~ size^-0.36, consistent across all 5 metros) PROVES the small-bay premium — extrapolated to a 40,000 SF ORA-sized building it implies ~+43%, independently matching the $160-220/SF band separate sources reported. The guide EXCLUDES land and soft costs, so it is a HARD-COST figure, not all-in. operative_benchmark_psf is DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED — swapping the basis gate is a governor-level decision requiring Gabriel's sign-off (see replacement_cost_doctrine.the_decision).

replacement_cost_doctrine.status: SUPERSEDED 2026-07-14 (SAME DAY). This file no longer carries an operative basis benchmark. THE SINGLE DENOMINATOR IS **RCT v03**, in the acquisition-underwriting skill (per-metro LOW/POINT/HIGH; basis divides by LOW; floor = linear vintage ramp 65% at <=1995 -> 60% at >=2005). This block is retained ONLY as the audit trail of how RCT v03 was sourced. DO NOT SCREEN OFF ANYTHING IN THIS FILE.
replacement_cost_doctrine.what_happened: On the morning of 2026-07-14 a C&W-hard-cost benchmark was ratified here as the operative basis gate. By the afternoon it was RETIRED, because reading the acquisition-underwriting skill properly revealed that ORA ALREADY had a replacement-cost doctrine (RCT v02) that was a better instrument on every axis: all-in rather than hard-cost-only, shallow-bay rather than big-box, 2026 rather than March-2025, banded, vintage-ramped, with an adder schedule. Ratifying a C&W benchmark here created a SECOND competing denominator — and two denominators is the actual bug. The C&W guide's correct role is (a) the PRIMARY SOURCE that RCT v03 is rebuilt from, and (b) the COHERENCE CHECK that exposed RCT v02's error. It is not itself a benchmark.
replacement_cost_doctrine.the_error_C_and_W_caught: RCT v02 claimed to be ALL-IN yet, for FIVE of nine markets, its all-in POINT sat BELOW C&W's pure HARD cost for the same metro (Cincinnati 134.00 < 143.15; Indianapolis 130.50 < 143.46; Grand Rapids 120.00 < 143.64; Richmond 131.50 < 133.70; Des Moines 130.00 < 131.46). All-in cannot be less than hard cost. RCT v02 had been scaled off a big-box baseline with the shallow-bay premium never applied — understating replacement, which made the discount test too strict, which meant ORA was PASSING ON DEALS THAT CLEAR DOCTRINE. Maryland ran the other way: RCT v02 priced it as the firm's most expensive market ($165) when C&W shows Baltimore is mid-priced ($133.70) — so the MD floor had been too GENEROUS.
replacement_cost_doctrine.why_this_matters: The basis hard floor is the PRIMARY gate on every acquisition. The replacement-cost figure IS the gate. It must have exactly one home. That home is RCT v03.

primary_source.what_it_measures: GROUND-UP BUILD-TO-SUIT DISTRIBUTION CENTERS, core & shell. 'Total Cost' = Site Work + Base Bldg Structural & Enclosure + Base Bldg Architectural + Base Bldg MEP + GC's/GR's & Fee + Contingency.
primary_source.what_it_EXCLUDES: LAND PURCHASE and SOFT COSTS (stated on its own page 2), plus FF&E, IT, A/V, security. It is therefore a HARD-COST figure, NOT all-in.

replacement_cost_doctrine.verdict_on_the_old_benchmarks: Our unsourced $140 Midwest was a GOOD hard-cost proxy — within ~7% of the real C&W figures (Columbus $130.51, KC $129.94, Cincinnati $143.15, Indianapolis $143.46). Our $170 MARYLAND was 27% TOO HIGH as a hard-cost figure — Baltimore is $133.70. That error made the MD basis floor too generous, and two Baltimore deals were wrongly cleared on the 2026-07-14 scan (700 Kane St at $115.38 and 2800 Annapolis Rd at $126.53 both FAIL against a C&W-hard benchmark).

the_small_bay_premium_is_REAL_and_the_gu.finding: The guide's own three size tiers imply cost scales as size^-0.36 (fitted exponent is 0.349-0.364 across all 5 ORA metros — remarkably consistent). Extrapolating that curve DOWN to a 40,000 SF ORA-sized building gives roughly +43% over the small-tier figure: Columbus ~$187, Cincinnati ~$205, Kansas City ~$186, Indianapolis ~$207, Baltimore ~$190.
the_small_bay_premium_is_REAL_and_the_gu.caution: That is an extrapolation BELOW the observed data range — directional, not underwriting-grade. But it independently lands in the $160-220/SF band that separate small-bay sources (Bisnow/Penntex Sept 2025; NAIOP Spring 2026) reported. Two independent lines of evidence agree.
the_small_bay_premium_is_REAL_and_the_gu.implication: TRUE all-in replacement for ORA's product (small-bay premium + soft costs + land) is plausibly $200-240/SF in the Midwest — far above anything we have been using.

the_decision.question: What does the basis floor test AGAINST — hard cost, or all-in (hard + soft + land)?
the_decision.RULING: GABRIEL RATIFIED HARD COST, 2026-07-14. The basis floor tests against C&W small-tier HARD COST, per metro.
the_decision.the_trap_this_avoids: All-in is the theoretically correct denominator (an existing building comes WITH its land). BUT modelling all-in at ~$230/SF Midwest sets the 25%-discount floor at <=$172/SF, which EVERY ONE of the 17 priced Midwest/MD deals on the 2026-07-14 scan clears. A floor that passes 17 of 17 is not a floor — it stops discriminating and the basis-buyer discipline evaporates.
the_decision.why_hard_cost_is_the_right_gate: It is SOURCED and dated; it is deliberately CONSERVATIVE (excluding land and soft costs, and priced for a building 1.4x-10x larger than ORA's, it UNDERSTATES true replacement — so the floor is HARDER to clear and we never overpay on a bad basis); it preserves week-over-week continuity; and it fixes the one real error (Maryland was 27% too generous).
the_decision.the_all_in_number_is_still_true_but_it_i: True all-in replacement for ORA product (small-bay premium + soft + land) is plausibly $200-240/SF Midwest. That is a legitimate IC-MEMO point — 'we are buying at 30-50% of true replacement cost' — and it should be USED in memos and lender packages. It is NOT the screening threshold. Do not let a big denominator dissolve the screen.

replacement_cost_doctrine.remaining_gaps: Even with the guide in hand, TWO of the three all-in components are still unsourced: (a) SOFT-COST percentage (assumed ~20%, never verified) and (b) LAND $/acre by submarket. If Gabriel rules for an all-in basis, both must be sourced before the floor can be trusted. A GC or lender quote per core market on a 30-50K SF shallow-bay build would settle hard cost, soft costs, and the small-bay premium in one stroke — still the highest-value two emails available.
replacement_cost_doctrine.staleness_warning: The C&W figures are MARCH 2025 costs. Construction cost has reaccelerated since: Turner Building Cost Index +4.87% YoY (Q1 2026); Mortenson +6.77% YoY; AGC nonresidential input PPI +8.4% YoY through May 2026 on tariff-driven steel (+20.7%), aluminum (+33.0%), copper (+20.9%). Expect the 2026 guide to print higher. Note the guide's OWN YoY moves were mostly NEGATIVE (Cincinnati -11.5%, Cleveland -14.3%, Columbus -7.7%) because the 2024->2025 industrial pipeline slowed — that trend has since reversed. RE-CHECK ANNUALLY on publication; inflate by a construction index in between.

changelog_1_5: RETIRED the operative basis benchmark from this file entirely. THERE IS NOW EXACTLY ONE DENOMINATOR: **RCT v03**, in the acquisition-underwriting skill. Reading that skill properly revealed ORA ALREADY had a replacement-cost doctrine (RCT v02) that beat the C&W benchmark on every axis — all-in not hard-cost-only, shallow-bay not big-box, 2026 not March-2025, banded, vintage-ramped, with an adder schedule and a renovation effective-vintage rule. Ratifying a C&W benchmark HERE had created a SECOND competing denominator, and two denominators was the actual bug. BUT RCT v02 was itself broken, and C&W is what proved it: for 5 of 9 markets RCT v02's ALL-IN point sat BELOW C&W's pure HARD cost (Cincinnati/Indianapolis/Grand Rapids/Richmond/Des Moines) — arithmetically impossible, since all-in contains hard cost. RCT v02 had been scaled off a big-box baseline with the shallow-bay premium never applied. RCT v03 (ratified 2026-07-14, Gabriel) rebuilds it from the C&W primary source: POINT = C&W hard x shallow-bay size premium (from C&W's OWN size curve, ~+43% at 40K SF) x soft/profit/financing 1.30x [EST — the one unsourced input, low end chosen deliberately so the floor stays hard] x escalation 1.0487 [Turner BCI, lowest of 3 indices]. Coherence now passes: every all-in exceeds hard cost at ~1.95x. The vintage ramp was RECALIBRATED 30/25 -> 65/60, because the floor%% and the denominator are a MATCHED PAIR — leaving 30%% against the corrected table would have set the Columbus floor at $160.76/SF, which every buy-box candidate clears. A floor that passes everything is not a floor. ORA's revealed selectivity implies a ~64%% discount to TRUE replacement: we buy at ~35-40%% of all-in replacement cost. The '25%% discount' language was always an artifact of a wrong denominator. Net per-market: Maryland TIGHTENS ~23%% (was the most over-generous), Grand Rapids LOOSENS ~16%% and Indianapolis ~7%% (both had been unfairly harsh), Columbus/KC/Madison tighten modestly, Richmond/Des Moines ~flat. Re-screen of the 2026-07-14 scan: 11 of 29 priced candidates now clear (a gate that discriminates).
